sla_notes_intro: Literature is the body of imaginative writing and oral art that expresses human experience through language. Four concepts are basic in its study: society, artist, imagination and literary language.
sla_notes_details: Society is the source of literary subject matter and the audience that receives it; the artist (writer or oral performer) observes society and shapes experiences into art; imagination is the creative power that lets the artist invent characters, events and worlds beyond literal fact; literary language is language used artistically, with imagery, symbolism, figures of speech and rhythm, to create effects. Learners discuss how the four interact and illustrate with examples from texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: A poet observes the suffering of farmers in drought (society), imagines the land as a dying mother (imagination) and writes: The earth, our mother, lies dry and silent (literary language).
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding these concepts helps students appreciate songs, stories, films and poems as reflections of the life around them.
sla_exercise: Define literature.::Imaginative artistic use of language, written or oral, to express human experience.||What is the role of the artist?::To observe society and shape experiences into a work of art.||Why is imagination important in literature?::It enables the creation of characters, events and settings beyond literal fact.||Give one feature of literary language.::Imagery or figures of speech such as metaphor.

sla_notes_intro: Folklore is the traditional knowledge, beliefs, customs and oral art passed from generation to generation among a community.
sla_notes_details: It is communal, anonymous, transmitted orally, flexible and functional. Its forms include folktales, myths, legends, proverbs, riddles, songs, lullabies, incantations, dances and customs. Functions of folklore include teaching morals, entertaining, preserving history, controlling behaviour and building unity. Folklore differs from written literature in medium, authorship and fixity.
sla_notes_illustrations: The Swahili proverb Haba na haba hujaza kibaba teaches patience and saving, and is transmitted orally through generations.
sla_notes_daily_life: Folklore is seen in grandmothers' storytelling, weddings, initiation rites and songs at community events.
sla_exercise: Define folklore.::Traditional knowledge, beliefs and oral art passed from generation to generation.||Name two forms of folklore.::Folktales and proverbs (or riddles, songs, myths).||Give two functions of folklore.::To teach morals and to entertain.||Why is folklore called anonymous?::The original authors are unknown; it belongs to the community.

sla_notes_intro: Genres are the main categories of written literature, based on form and conventions.
sla_notes_details: The three major genres are prose (novel, novella, short story, biography, autobiography), drama (tragedy, comedy, tragicomedy, melodrama and satire) and poetry (lyric, narrative, epic, ballad, elegy, ode and sonnet). Learners identify features of each genre, such as narration in prose, dialogue and acts in drama, and stanzas, verse, rhythm and rhyme in poetry, and classify sample texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet is classified as a tragedy in the drama genre, while Things Fall Apart belongs to prose as a novel.
sla_notes_daily_life: Classification helps readers to choose books and to understand what to expect from a work.
sla_exercise: Name the three major genres.::Prose, drama and poetry.||Give two forms of prose.::Novel and short story.||What is an elegy?::A poem of mourning for the dead.||Which genre is written for stage performance?::Drama.

sla_notes_intro: Imagery is the use of language that appeals to the senses to create mental pictures.
sla_notes_details: Types are visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory and kinaesthetic imagery. Writers also use symbolic imagery and figures such as simile and metaphor. Learners identify images in a selected work, explain what human experiences they reflect (fear, joy, poverty, hope, loss) and discuss their effect on mood and meaning.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the line: The cold wind bit through their thin blankets, tactile imagery reflects the hardship of poverty.
sla_notes_daily_life: Imagery is used in songs, advertisements and everyday speech to make expression vivid.
sla_exercise: Define imagery.::Language that appeals to the senses and creates mental pictures.||Name two types of imagery.::Visual and auditory.||What sense does tactile imagery appeal to?::Touch.||What does the line: the sun was a golden coin illustrate?::A visual metaphor.

sla_notes_intro: These theories explain the origins of literature: literature imitates life, arises from myths, or grows out of ritual.
sla_notes_details: The mimetic theory, associated with Plato and Aristotle, holds that literature imitates (mimesis) actions and life. The myth theory states that literature developed from myths that explain the world, gods and origins of humanity. The ritual theory states that drama and poetry began in religious rites, chants, dances and ceremonies performed by communities. Learners compare the assumptions of each.
sla_notes_illustrations: The dramatised story of creation in a traditional ceremony shows how ritual and myth can produce performance.
sla_notes_daily_life: Ceremonies, songs and stories in modern communities show how art and belief are linked.
sla_exercise: What does mimetic mean?::Imitating or representing life.||Who are the philosophers associated with mimesis?::Plato and Aristotle.||According to ritual theory, where did drama originate?::In religious rites and ceremonies.||What is a myth?::A traditional story that explains natural events, gods or origins.

sla_notes_intro: Elements such as plot, setting, resolution, conflict and characters may carry imitation, ritual and mythical features.
sla_notes_details: Learners read a selected work and identify how events imitate real life; how ceremonies (initiation, sacrifice, burial) shape plots and settings; how mythical characters and archetypes (hero, trickster, mother earth) function; and how conflict and resolution follow patterns of journey, struggle and renewal. They evaluate the contribution of these elements to meaning.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Things Fall Apart, the New Yam festival and the Week of Peace are ritual settings that show the community's values and are disrupted by the plot's conflict.
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising these elements shows how literature reflects shared beliefs and practices.
sla_exercise: Give an example of a ritual element in a novel.::A festival, sacrifice or burial ceremony.||What is an archetype?::A universal pattern or type of character or event.||How does ritual contribute to setting?::It gives cultural and religious background to events.||What is resolution?::The outcome of the conflict in a plot.

sla_notes_intro: The theories can be used to explain how forms of folklore and written literature developed.
sla_notes_details: Learners trace oral genres such as praise poetry, songs, dramatised rituals and myths and show how they gave rise to poetry, drama and narrative prose. Ritual chants developed into dramatic performances; myths became epic narrative; imitation of everyday life produced realism in the novel. They present the development from oral to written forms.
sla_notes_illustrations: Traditional harvest dances with songs and dramatic movement can be seen as forerunners of drama.
sla_notes_daily_life: This helps students see that modern theatre, film and music are rooted in ancient practices.

sla_notes_intro: African literature in English blends African oral traditions with Western literary conventions.
sla_notes_details: Oral traditions offer proverbs, storytelling techniques, songs, praise names, communal values and rhythmic language; Western conventions provide the novel, the play script, the sonnet and written publication. African writers combine them, using proverbs, folktales and idioms within English narratives, adapting English to African rhythms (indigenisation) and treating African subject matter.
sla_notes_illustrations: Chinua Achebe uses the proverb Proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten in an English novel, showing the fusion of traditions.
sla_notes_daily_life: The blend appears in modern songs, films and novels in which local languages and English mix.
sla_exercise: Give one oral feature used in African novels.::Proverbs or folktales.||What is a Western convention used by African authors?::The novel form (or the written play).||What is indigenisation of language?::Adapting English to express African culture.||Name a writer who uses proverbs in English.::Chinua Achebe.

sla_notes_intro: African authors developed literature in English that expresses African experiences and challenges colonial views.
sla_notes_details: Learners study writers such as Chinua Achebe, Wole Soyinka, Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Ama Ata Aidoo, Nadine Gordimer, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Okot p'Bitek and Buchi Emecheta, who wrote about traditional life, colonial encounter, independence, corruption, gender and identity. They discuss their themes, styles, and awards, and their role in giving voice to Africans and shaping world literature.
sla_notes_illustrations: Achebe's Things Fall Apart answered European portrayals of Africa by presenting Igbo society with dignity and complexity.
sla_notes_daily_life: African literature is used in schools, theatre and film and promotes cultural pride.

sla_notes_intro: Pre-colonial African literature is the literature produced before European colonisation, mainly oral.
sla_notes_details: Features include oral performance, communal authorship, use of proverbs, praise poetry, myths, legends, epics, folktales and songs, moral and educational purpose, audience participation, repetition and rhythm, and reflection of traditional values and religion. In selected works set in this period, learners identify these features and the society represented.
sla_notes_illustrations: The Epic of Sundiata from Mali was told by griots, with music and audience participation, praising the hero and teaching leadership.
sla_notes_daily_life: The features survive in storytelling, wedding songs and traditional ceremonies.
sla_exercise: How was pre-colonial literature mainly transmitted?::Orally.||Who is a griot?::A West African oral historian and praise singer.||Give two features of pre-colonial literature.::Use of proverbs and audience participation.||What was its main purpose?::To educate, entertain and preserve tradition.

sla_notes_intro: Colonial African literature was written during the period of colonial rule and reflects encounters between Africans and Europeans.
sla_notes_details: Its features include themes of cultural conflict, loss of land and identity, forced labour, taxation, mission education, resistance, and racial discrimination; use of English, French or Portuguese; mixture of oral and written forms; protest and assertion of African values. Learners study a selected work and identify these features and their historical background.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Things Fall Apart, the arrival of missionaries and the colonial court divides the Umuofia community and destroys traditional authority.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding colonial literature helps young people to appreciate the history behind present social conditions.
sla_exercise: Name one theme of colonial literature.::Cultural conflict.||What did colonial literature often protest?::Injustice, land loss and racial discrimination.||What language did many writers use?::The colonial language, such as English.||Why study colonial literature?::To understand history and cultural change.

sla_notes_intro: Post-colonial African literature is written after independence and addresses the problems and hopes of new nations.
sla_notes_details: Features include disillusionment with leadership, corruption, neo-colonialism, political violence, urban life, gender issues, migration, identity and language debates; experimental forms; and satire. Writers such as Ngugi, Soyinka and Ayi Kwei Armah criticise leaders and colonial legacy. Learners identify these features in a selected work.
sla_notes_illustrations: In A Man of the People by Achebe, a corrupt minister exploits ordinary citizens, showing post-independence disillusionment.
sla_notes_daily_life: The issues in this literature are found in current news on governance, gender and unemployment.

sla_notes_intro: These are the three broad categories of folklore.
sla_notes_details: Material culture includes physical objects made traditionally, such as tools, pottery, baskets, clothing, houses, food and crafts. Social folk custom includes customs and beliefs such as rites of passage (birth, initiation, marriage, death), festivals, taboos and hospitality. Performing folk arts include music, dance, drama, storytelling, songs and oral poetry. Learners describe examples from local communities.
sla_notes_illustrations: A Maasai beaded necklace is material culture; a wedding ceremony is a social folk custom; the Ngoma dance is a performing folk art.
sla_notes_daily_life: These categories are seen in local museums, cultural festivals and family celebrations.
sla_exercise: Give one example of material culture.::Pottery or baskets.||Which category includes marriage customs?::Social folk custom.||Give one performing folk art.::Ngoma dance or storytelling.||What is a taboo?::Something forbidden by custom.

sla_notes_details: Learners identify forms in their communities through observation, interviews and field research: folktales, riddles, proverbs, songs, dances, ceremonies, food, dress and arts and crafts. sla_notes_details: Learners identify songs, proverbs, folktales, myths, riddles, rituals and dances that appear in a selected text, explain how they are presented, and discuss their functions such as characterisation, theme development, authenticity, humour and moral teaching.

sla_notes_intro: Folklore and written literature influence and enrich each other.
sla_notes_details: Written literature borrows content, forms, characters, style and language from folklore; folklore also adopts materials from written sources. They differ in that folklore is oral, communal and flexible while written literature is authored and fixed. Learners compare the two and give examples of adaptations, such as folktales retold in books and films.
sla_notes_illustrations: The story of Sundiata, originally oral, has been published as written epic and adapted for film.
sla_notes_daily_life: Fables in textbooks and cartoons based on folktales are everyday examples.

sla_notes_intro: Elements of literature are the basic components that make up a literary work.
sla_notes_details: They include setting (time, place), theme (central idea), message (lesson conveyed), language (diction and figures), plot (arrangement of events), style (author's manner of writing) and characters (people in the work). Learners define each, identify them in sample texts and explain how they work together.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a story set in a poor village, where a boy struggles to attend school, the setting is the village, the theme is perseverance and the message is that determination leads to success.
sla_notes_daily_life: These elements are used to discuss films, series and stories that people consume daily.

sla_notes_intro: Each element has a role in creating the meaning and effect of a work.
sla_notes_details: Setting provides context and mood; characters embody ideas and drive action; plot organises events to create suspense; theme gives unity; language and style create beauty and voice; message educates. Learners choose a text, discuss the contribution of each element with quotations, and assess which elements are the strongest.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a play, a rural setting with drought heightens the conflict over water and reveals characters' true nature.
sla_notes_daily_life: Awareness of elements helps in judging books and films.

sla_notes_intro: Form is how a work is structured and expressed; content is what it is about.
sla_notes_details: Learners examine how form (structure, language, genre, point of view, tone) supports content (theme, message and subject matter). A serious theme may need a solemn tone and elevated diction, while satire uses exaggeration. Changing the form changes the effect. They analyse how a poem's short lines can show urgency, or how a first-person narrator adds intimacy.
sla_notes_illustrations: A poem about the passing of time in a regular, slow rhythm reinforces its solemn content.
sla_notes_daily_life: Form and content work together in songs and advertisements to deliver a message.
sla_exercise: Define form in literature.::The structure and manner of expression of a work.||Define content.::The subject matter and ideas of a work.||How can short lines affect a poem?::They can create urgency.||Give one example of form supporting content.::A solemn tone for a serious theme.

learning_activity_name: Examine the four traditional critical theories (mimetic, pragmatic, objective and expressive)
sla_name: Four traditional critical theories
sla_assessment_criteria: The four traditional critical theories are well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio-visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Traditional literary criticism developed four major approaches identified by M. H. Abrams.
sla_notes_details: The mimetic theory judges literature by how well it represents the world; the pragmatic theory judges it by its effect on the audience (teaching and pleasing); the objective theory judges it as a self-contained work by its internal form; the expressive theory judges it as an expression of the author's feelings and personality. Learners explain each and apply it to a poem or play.
sla_notes_illustrations: A critic who asks whether the novel truthfully portrays village life is using the mimetic approach.
sla_notes_daily_life: These approaches appear when people review films, books and songs.
sla_exercise: Name the four traditional theories.::Mimetic, pragmatic, objective and expressive.||What does the pragmatic theory focus on?::The effect on the audience.||What does the expressive theory focus on?::The author's feelings and imagination.||Which theory looks only at the work's internal form?::The objective theory.

specific_competence_name: Analyse literary criticism theories
learning_activity_name: Explain modern theories of literary criticism (formalism, Marxism, post-colonial, feminism, eco-criticism and social learning theory)
sla_name: Modern theories of literary criticism
sla_assessment_criteria: Modern theories of literary criticism are explained clearly.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Modern theories offer new lenses for interpreting literature.
sla_notes_details: Formalism focuses on form and language; Marxism on class and economic power; post-colonialism on colonial legacy and identity; feminism on gender relations and women's representation; eco-criticism on the relationship between literature and the natural environment; and social learning theory on how audiences learn behaviour by observing characters. Learners state the principles of each and their key concerns.
sla_notes_illustrations: An eco-critical reading of a poem on deforestation examines how nature is represented and what attitude to the environment is promoted.
sla_notes_daily_life: These theories help to analyse current social, political and environmental issues in media.
sla_exercise: What does Marxist criticism examine?::Class and economic power.||What does eco-criticism study?::Literature and the natural environment.||What is social learning theory?::The idea that people learn by observing and imitating models.||What is the concern of post-colonial theory?::Colonial legacy, identity and resistance.

specific_competence_name: Analyse literary criticism theories
learning_activity_name: Apply modern literary theories in critiquing a selected literary text
sla_name: Applying modern literary theories in critiquing a text
sla_assessment_criteria: Modern literary theories are applied effectively in critiquing a selected literary text.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Applying a theory means using its principles to analyse and interpret a chosen text.
sla_notes_details: Steps: read the text, choose a suitable theory, define its main concepts, identify relevant characters, events and language, interpret them through the theory, support with evidence and make a conclusion. A critique should be balanced, logical and well organised, and may compare interpretations from different theories.
sla_notes_illustrations: Using feminist theory on a novel where the wife has no say in family decisions, the critic argues that patriarchy limits women.
sla_notes_daily_life: Critical reading skills apply to interpreting news, films and social debates.
sla_exercise: Give the first step in applying a theory.::Reading the text carefully.||Why give evidence?::To justify the interpretation.||Name one theory suitable for a novel about class conflict.::Marxist theory.||What should a critique conclude with?::A balanced judgment.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Apply formalism theory in analysing a selected literary text
sla_name: Applying formalism in analysing a literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Formalism theory is applied effectively in analysing the form of a selected literary text.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio-visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Formalism analyses a text as an independent work, focusing on its language, structure and devices.
sla_notes_details: Formalist critics study diction, imagery, symbolism, irony, paradox, tone, structure, plot pattern, point of view and rhythm, and how these produce unity and meaning without depending on the author's life or history. Learners perform close reading of a poem or passage, identifying devices and explaining their effects.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a poem, repeated words for darkness and the closing image of a lit candle show a movement from despair to hope, discovered through close reading.
sla_notes_daily_life: Close reading develops attention to language in contracts, speeches and media texts.
sla_exercise: What is formalism?::A theory analysing the text's form and language on their own.||What is close reading?::Careful detailed analysis of a text's language and structure.||Name one device formalists study.::Imagery or irony.||Does formalism depend on the author's biography?::No, it focuses on the text itself.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Apply modern literary theories to discuss thematic representation in selected pre-colonial and colonial literary texts
sla_name: Thematic representation in pre-colonial and colonial texts
sla_method: Think-Ink-Pair-Share and Engagement with a text
sla_assessment_criteria: Modern literary theories are applied effectively to discuss thematic representation in selected pre-colonial and colonial literary texts.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Themes are the central ideas that literary texts explore, and modern theories help to discuss them.
sla_notes_details: Learners select pre-colonial and colonial texts and identify themes such as tradition, communal life, courage, leadership, cultural conflict, religion, land and resistance. They apply theories such as Marxism (land and labour), post-colonialism (cultural domination) or feminism (women's roles) to discuss how the themes are presented through characters, plot and language.
sla_notes_illustrations: A post-colonial reading of a colonial text shows the theme of cultural domination in the missionaries' attitude to local religion.
sla_notes_daily_life: Analysing themes helps citizens to understand the roots of present-day social issues.
sla_exercise: Give two themes of colonial literature.::Cultural conflict and resistance.||Which theory suits themes of cultural domination?::Post-colonial theory.||How are themes presented?::Through characters, plot and language.||Why apply theories to themes?::To interpret them systematically.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Relate issues represented in selected pre-colonial and colonial literary texts to real life experiences
sla_name: Relating issues in pre-colonial and colonial texts to real life
sla_assessment_criteria: Issues represented in selected pre-colonial and colonial literary texts.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Issues in early literary texts still echo in society today.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify issues such as land disputes, forced labour, discrimination, leadership, cultural erosion and gender roles, and connect them to modern situations such as land conflicts, labour rights and cultural preservation. They discuss causes, effects and possible solutions with evidence from the text and community experience.
sla_notes_illustrations: The land seizure in a colonial novel can be related to present land conflicts and the need for fair land laws.
sla_notes_daily_life: The connections help students to become informed and responsible citizens.
sla_exercise: Give one issue that links colonial texts to modern life.::Land conflicts.||Why relate texts to real life?::To understand their relevance.||What kind of evidence supports the link?::Quotations and real examples.||Name a possible solution to land conflicts.::Fair laws and dialogue.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Discern lessons obtained in selected pre-colonial and colonial literary texts
sla_name: Lessons from pre-colonial and colonial literary texts
sla_assessment_criteria: Lessons obtained in selected pre-colonial and colonial literary texts are well discerned.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Discerning lessons means identifying the moral and social teachings in the texts.
sla_notes_details: Learners read texts and infer lessons such as the value of unity, respect for culture, the dangers of pride, the need for adaptability, the price of injustice and the importance of education. They explain how the characters' fortunes lead to the lessons and state them in complete sentences.
sla_notes_illustrations: Okonkwo's downfall in Things Fall Apart teaches that inflexibility and excessive pride can destroy a person.
sla_notes_daily_life: Lessons from these texts guide personal and community decisions.
sla_exercise: State a lesson from Okonkwo's downfall.::Excessive pride and rigidity lead to ruin.||How are lessons discerned?::From characters' actions and their consequences.||Give another lesson from colonial texts.::Unity is strength.||Why must lessons be supported?::With evidence from the text.

specific_competence_name: Use literary works to build rational arguments and judgment
learning_activity_name: Explain the principles for making rational argument and judgment in literature
sla_name: Principles for making rational arguments and judgments in literature
sla_assessment_criteria: Principles for making rational argument and judgment are explained correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio-visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A rational argument is a reasoned position supported by evidence, and judgment is a considered evaluation.
sla_notes_details: Principles include stating a clear claim, supporting it with textual evidence, using logical reasoning, avoiding fallacies (such as personal attack, overgeneralisation and false cause), considering counter-arguments, using precise language and reaching a fair conclusion. Learners apply them in essays and debates on literary questions.
sla_notes_illustrations: Claim: Okonkwo is a tragic hero. Evidence: His greatness and his fatal flaw of fear of weakness lead to his fall.
sla_notes_daily_life: Rational argument skills are valuable in law, politics and everyday debates.
sla_exercise: What is a claim?::The main point that an argument supports.||Name a logical fallacy.::Overgeneralisation or personal attack.||Why consider counter-arguments?::To make the argument stronger and fairer.||What supports a claim in literary analysis?::Evidence from the text.

specific_competence_name: Use literary works to build rational arguments and judgment
learning_activity_name: Discuss the actions of the characters in a selected literary text
sla_name: Actions of characters in a selected literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: The actions of the characters in a selected literary text are well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Characters' actions reveal their personalities, values and motives and drive the plot.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify types of characters (protagonist, antagonist, round, flat, dynamic, static), study their actions and speech, and judge whether the actions are justified and consistent. They examine the consequences and what the actions teach about human nature, using evidence from the text to form opinions.
sla_notes_illustrations: When a character shares her small food with a hungry neighbour despite being poor, her action reveals generosity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Judging actions in stories trains learners to make wise choices in their own lives.
sla_exercise: What is a protagonist?::The main character.||What does a dynamic character do?::Changes during the story.||How do actions reveal character?::They show values and motives.||Give one way of judging an action.::By its motives and consequences.

learning_activity_name: Analyse the themes portrayed in a selected literary text
sla_name: Themes portrayed in a selected literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: The themes portrayed in a selected literary text are correctly analysed.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A theme is the central idea or underlying message in a text.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify major and minor themes such as love, betrayal, power, poverty, identity, freedom, corruption and education. They trace how the themes develop through plot, characters, symbols and language, and evaluate their relevance. Each theme must be expressed in a full statement, not a single word, and supported by evidence.
sla_notes_illustrations: Theme statement: Greed for power destroys relationships, evidenced by the brothers' quarrel over the throne.
sla_notes_daily_life: Themes in literature reflect social issues such as governance, family and justice.
sla_exercise: Define theme.::The central idea in a text.||Give a theme statement about power.::Abuse of power leads to suffering.||How do symbols support themes?::They represent abstract ideas.||Difference between major and minor themes?::Major themes dominate the work, minor ones are secondary.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the principles of composing literary works
learning_activity_name: Distinguish writing for children and writing for adults
sla_name: Writing for children and writing for adults
sla_assessment_criteria: Writing for children and writing for adults are correctly distinguished.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio-visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Literature for children differs from that for adults in content, language and purpose.
sla_notes_details: Children's writing uses simple vocabulary, short sentences, clear plots, familiar settings, animal or child characters, illustrations, repetition, humour and clear moral lessons, and avoids disturbing themes. Adult writing uses complex language, sophisticated themes such as politics, sex, war, and moral ambiguity, and longer structures. Learners compare sample texts and consider the age and needs of the audience.
sla_notes_illustrations: A children's story about a clever hare uses simple words and repetition, while an adult novel about corruption uses layered symbolism and irony.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding this helps teachers, parents and writers to choose suitable books for children.
sla_exercise: Give one feature of children's literature.::Simple language and clear morals.||Give one feature of adult literature.::Complex themes.||Why are illustrations used for children?::To support understanding and attract attention.||Why consider audience when writing?::To make content and language suitable.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the principles of composing literary works
learning_activity_name: Discuss the principles of composing a work of literature (point of view, characterisation, plot and conflict)
sla_name: Principles of composing a work of literature
sla_assessment_criteria: The principles of composing a literary work are well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Composing literature requires attention to point of view, characterisation, plot and conflict.
sla_notes_details: Point of view may be first person, third person limited or omniscient; characterisation is done by description, speech, actions and others' opinions; plot should have a beginning, middle and end with cause-and-effect links; conflict (internal, interpersonal, social or with nature) creates tension. Consistency, originality, unity and vivid language are also required.
sla_notes_illustrations: A first-person narrator telling about her fear during a flood gives immediacy and lets the reader feel her emotions.
sla_notes_daily_life: These principles help in storytelling, scriptwriting and creative projects.
sla_exercise: Name three points of view.::First person, third person and omniscient.||What is characterisation?::The way a writer presents and develops characters.||Why is conflict essential in a plot?::It creates tension and moves the story.||Give two methods of characterisation.::Description and dialogue.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the principles of composing literary works
learning_activity_name: Elaborate the steps for writing a short story (pre-writing, writing, revision, editing and publishing)
sla_name: Steps for writing a short story
sla_assessment_criteria: The steps for writing a short story are well elaborated.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A short story is a brief prose narrative focusing on a single incident or idea.
sla_notes_details: The steps are pre-writing (choosing an idea, brainstorming, planning characters, setting and plot), writing the first draft (opening, rising action, climax, ending), revision (improving content and structure), editing (correcting grammar, spelling and punctuation) and publishing (sharing in a magazine, book or online). The writer keeps unity of effect and few characters.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student brainstorms a story about a boy who finds a lost wallet, drafts the events, revises the ending and publishes it in the school magazine.
sla_notes_daily_life: The process applies to any writing task, such as essays and reports.
sla_exercise: List the steps of writing a short story.::Pre-writing, writing, revision, editing and publishing.||What is done in revision?::Improving content, structure and clarity.||What is done in editing?::Correcting grammar, spelling and punctuation.||Where can a story be published?::In magazines, books or online.

specific_competence_name: Compose original literary works
learning_activity_name: Develop a plan for composing a short story (idea, plot, setting and characterisation)
sla_name: Planning a short story
sla_assessment_criteria: A plan for composing a short story is well developed.
sla_teaching_aids: ICT tools
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A plan sets out the idea, plot, setting and characters before writing.
sla_notes_details: The writer decides the central idea, the main character and his or her goal, the obstacles, the setting, the point of view, and the sequence of events leading to climax and ending. A story map or outline summarising each stage of the plot is prepared, and character profiles are written to keep details consistent.
sla_notes_illustrations: Plan: Idea - honesty; Character - Juma, a shopkeeper's son; Conflict - he finds extra money in change; Climax - he must decide; Ending - he returns the money and gains trust.
sla_notes_daily_life: Planning helps in organising presentations and projects.
sla_exercise: Name four things to include in a story plan.::Idea, plot, setting and characters.||What is a story map?::An outline of the story's events.||Why write character profiles?::To keep details consistent.||What is the climax?::The turning point of the story.

specific_competence_name: Compose original literary works
learning_activity_name: Apply basic skills in creative writing to compose a short story
sla_name: Basic creative writing skills in composing a short story
sla_assessment_criteria: Basic skills in creative writing are correctly applied in composing a short story.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Creative writing skills enable a writer to compose engaging stories.
sla_notes_details: Skills include a strong opening hook, showing rather than telling, vivid description, realistic dialogue, varied sentence structure, suspense, use of figurative language, consistent point of view and a satisfying ending. Learners write a draft, read aloud, get peer feedback and improve.
sla_notes_illustrations: Instead of writing: It was cold, one may write: Her teeth chattered as the wind pushed through the cracks in the wall.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills also improve descriptive essays, speeches and social media content.
sla_exercise: What is a hook?::An opening that attracts the reader's interest.||What does showing rather than telling mean?::Using details and action instead of direct statements.||Why use dialogue?::To reveal character and move the story.||Why get peer feedback?::To identify weaknesses and improve the work.

sla_name: Using ICT tools to write and publish a short story

sla_notes_intro: ICT tools help writers to compose, edit, illustrate and publish stories.
sla_notes_details: Word processors allow drafting, spell-check, formatting and version history; online storage and collaboration tools such as shared documents allow co-writing and feedback; graphics tools allow illustrations and cover design; and digital platforms such as blogs, e-book sites, school websites and social media allow publication. Writers must respect copyright, avoid plagiarism and protect personal safety online.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student types a story in a word processor, adds an illustration, converts it to PDF and publishes it on the school website.
sla_notes_daily_life: Digital publishing gives young writers a wide audience and creates income opportunities.
sla_exercise: Name one ICT tool for writing.::A word processor.||Where can a story be published online?::A blog or e-book platform.||What is plagiarism?::Copying another's work without acknowledgement.||Why respect copyright?::To protect the rights of creators.

learning_activity_name: Discuss how the aspects of indigenous socio-cultural setting, Ujamaa and Pan-Africanism have influenced Tanzanian Literature in English
sla_name: Indigenous culture, Ujamaa and Pan-Africanism in Tanzanian literature
sla_assessment_criteria: The influence of aspects of indigenous socio-cultural setting, Ujamaa and Pan-Africanism on Tanzanian Literature in English are well discussed.

sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Tanzanian literature in English has been shaped by indigenous socio-cultural settings and by the ideologies of Ujamaa and Pan-Africanism.
sla_notes_details: Indigenous culture provides oral traditions, proverbs, communal values and Kiswahili influence. Ujamaa, the policy of African socialism promoted by Julius Nyerere after 1967, emphasised communal living, equality, self-reliance and work, and its themes appear in the works of writers such as Ebrahim Hussein and Penina Muhando. Pan-Africanism stressed African unity, liberation and dignity and inspired themes of solidarity and resistance. Learners discuss these influences with textual examples.
sla_notes_illustrations: A play that criticises selfish individuals who refuse to join the communal village project reflects the values of Ujamaa.
sla_notes_daily_life: These ideologies still influence national values such as unity, cooperation and self-reliance.
sla_exercise: What is Ujamaa?::Tanzania's policy of African socialism emphasising communal life and self-reliance.||Who was its main promoter?::Julius Nyerere.||Give one theme inspired by Pan-Africanism.::African unity and liberation.||Name one indigenous influence on Tanzanian literature.::Oral traditions, proverbs or Kiswahili.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts and principles of literature
specific_competence_name: Assess the contribution of Tanzanian writers to the development of Tanzanian literature in English

sla_assessment_criteria: Development of Tanzanian Literature in English is sufficiently surveyed.

sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Tanzanian literature in English developed from the colonial period to the present, alongside a strong Kiswahili literary tradition.
sla_notes_details: Early works appeared in the colonial and independence periods, with growth in the 1960s and 1970s in universities and publishing houses such as the East African Publishing House. Learners survey pioneers and genres: poems by Tanzanian poets, plays by Ebrahim Hussein (Kinjeketile) and Penina Muhando, novels by Peter Palangyo (Dying in the Sun), William Kamera, Abdulrazak Gurnah and Elieshi Lema, and identify phases, themes and challenges such as publishing and language choice.
sla_notes_illustrations: Dying in the Sun by Peter Palangyo (1968) is among the early Tanzanian novels in English and explores the relationship between a son and his father.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of the development inspires new writers and readers to support local literature.
sla_exercise: Name one Tanzanian novelist writing in English.::Peter Palangyo, Abdulrazak Gurnah or Elieshi Lema.||Name one Tanzanian playwright.::Ebrahim Hussein or Penina Muhando.||What was one challenge for early writers?::Limited publishing opportunities.||Which decade saw growth in Tanzanian literature?::The 1960s and 1970s.

sla_notes_intro: Tanzanian authors reflect the nation's cultural, social and political heritage in their works.
sla_notes_details: Using a selected text, learners examine how the author portrays traditions, customs and values, colonial and independence history, social structures such as family and community, and political events such as the struggle for independence and Ujamaa. They analyse language, characters and setting to show the author's attitude and evaluate how the text preserves national memory.
sla_notes_illustrations: Kinjeketile by Ebrahim Hussein dramatises the Maji Maji resistance, reflecting national political and cultural heritage.
sla_notes_daily_life: Such texts help citizens to remember history and value their identity.
sla_exercise: Which uprising is dramatised in Kinjeketile?::The Maji Maji uprising.||What does heritage mean?::Traditions and history inherited from the past.||Give one way an author reflects culture.::By presenting customs and values through characters.||Why is this important?::It preserves national memory and identity.

sla_notes_intro: Tanzanian writers respond to current issues in society through their works.
sla_notes_details: Learners examine how authors represent issues such as corruption, gender inequality, taxation, development, unemployment, HIV/AIDS, environmental degradation, digital technology and youth. They study techniques such as satire, realism, symbolism and characterisation, and discuss the effectiveness of the works in raising awareness and proposing solutions.
sla_notes_illustrations: A short story about a civil servant who takes bribes and is finally exposed raises awareness about the effects of corruption on development.
sla_notes_daily_life: Literature gives citizens a voice on social issues and motivates positive change.
sla_exercise: Name two topical issues covered by writers.::Corruption and gender inequality.||Which technique is used to criticise vices humorously?::Satire.||How does literature raise awareness?::By dramatising problems and their effects.||Why is taxation a topical issue?::It relates to national development and citizen responsibilities.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Examine the effectiveness of narrative techniques, and literary devices in a selected literary text
sla_name: Narrative techniques and literary devices in a selected text
sla_assessment_criteria: Effectiveness of narrative techniques, and various literary devices used in a selected literary text is well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio- visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Narrative techniques are the methods a writer uses to tell a story, and literary devices are the tools used to create effects.
sla_notes_details: Narrative techniques include point of view, flashback, foreshadowing, stream of consciousness, framing narrative, dialogue, and irony. Devices include symbolism, imagery, allusion, motif, metaphor and irony. Learners judge effectiveness by considering how each technique creates suspense, reveals character, develops theme or shapes the reader's response, giving quotations.
sla_notes_illustrations: A flashback in a novel that shows a character's childhood trauma helps explain her adult fear of commitment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising techniques improves understanding of films, novels and even news storytelling.
sla_exercise: What is foreshadowing?::A hint of events to come.||What is a flashback?::A scene showing an earlier event.||What is a motif?::A recurring element that supports theme.||How do you judge the effectiveness of a device?::By its impact on meaning and effect on the reader.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Apply modern literary theories to discuss thematic representation in selected liberation and post-colonial literary texts
sla_name: Thematic representation in liberation and post-colonial texts
sla_assessment_criteria: Modern literary theories are applied correctly in discussing thematic representation in selected liberation and post-colonial literary texts.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Liberation and post-colonial texts explore themes of freedom, struggle, disillusionment and rebuilding.
sla_notes_details: Learners study themes such as the fight for independence, sacrifice, betrayal by leaders, corruption, neo-colonialism, identity, exile, gender and reconstruction. They apply theories such as Marxism, post-colonialism, feminism and eco-criticism to interpret how the themes are presented through plot, character and language, with evidence.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Ngugi's A Grain of Wheat, the theme of betrayal in the struggle for independence is presented through Mugo's guilt.
sla_notes_daily_life: The themes correspond to current debates on governance and justice.
sla_exercise: Name one liberation theme.::Struggle for freedom.||What is neo-colonialism?::Continuing economic or political control by foreign powers after independence.||Which theory looks at gender in a text?::Feminist theory.||Who wrote A Grain of Wheat?::Ngugi wa Thiong'o.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Relate issues represented in selected liberation and post-colonial literary texts to real life experiences
sla_name: Relating issues in liberation and post-colonial texts to real life
sla_assessment_criteria: Issues represented in selected liberation and post-colonial literary texts are well related to real life experiences.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Issues in liberation and post-colonial texts remain relevant in contemporary societies.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify issues such as political violence, corruption, unequal distribution of resources, gender oppression, youth unemployment and refugees, and relate them to real events in Africa. They discuss root causes, consequences and solutions such as democracy, education and accountability, and present findings in essays or debates.
sla_notes_illustrations: The corrupt ministers in post-independence novels remind us of real cases of embezzlement of public funds.
sla_notes_daily_life: Relating texts to life makes learners more responsible citizens.
sla_exercise: Give an issue in post-colonial texts that exists today.::Corruption.||Name one solution to corruption.::Accountability and strong laws.||Why compare fiction with real life?::To see its relevance and learn lessons.||What is embezzlement?::Stealing funds entrusted to one's care.

specific_competence_name: Analyse critically pre-colonial, colonial, liberation, and post-colonial literatures
learning_activity_name: Reflect on characters’ experiences in selected liberation and post-colonial literary texts
sla_name: Characters' experiences in liberation and post-colonial texts
sla_assessment_criteria: Characters’ experiences in liberation and post-colonial literary texts are well reflected on.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Reflecting on characters' experiences means considering how characters live through, suffer and respond to historical events.
sla_notes_details: Learners study the experiences of freedom fighters, ordinary citizens, women, exiles and leaders, analyse their motives, emotions, choices and transformation, and reflect on what these experiences say about the human condition and history. They write character studies and personal reflections supported by textual evidence.
sla_notes_illustrations: A freedom fighter who returns home to find that independence has not brought justice experiences disillusionment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding characters' experiences develops empathy for people who face hardship.
sla_exercise: What is disillusionment?::Disappointment on discovering that something is not as good as expected.||What is a character study?::A detailed analysis of a character.||Why reflect on characters' experiences?::To develop empathy and understanding.||Give one experience of characters in liberation texts.::Sacrifice or suffering.

specific_competence_name: Analyse the nexus between literature and politics, aesthetics and social inequalities
learning_activity_name: Examine the representation of political issues (human rights, good governance, election, etc) in a selected literary text
sla_name: Representation of political issues in a literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Representation of political issues in a selected literary text is well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio- visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Literature represents political issues such as human rights, good governance and elections.
sla_notes_details: Learners examine how a selected text depicts abuse of power, one-party rule, electoral malpractice, censorship, imprisonment of dissidents, accountability and citizens' participation. They analyse techniques such as satire, allegory, symbolism and irony and discuss the author's political stance.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Animal Farm, the pigs' takeover symbolises how leaders can betray the ideals of a revolution.
sla_notes_daily_life: The analysis helps citizens to participate knowledgeably in elections and governance.
sla_exercise: What is allegory?::A story with a hidden political or moral meaning.||Name one political issue in literature.::Human rights or elections.||How does satire criticise leaders?::By mocking their faults humorously.||What is good governance?::Fair, transparent and accountable leadership.

specific_competence_name: Analyse the nexus between literature and politics, aesthetics and social inequalities
learning_activity_name: Examine the depiction of social inequalities (racial discrimination, wage inequality, homelessness, inequality in education, etc) in a selected literary text
sla_name: Depiction of social inequalities in a literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Depiction of social inequalities in a selected literary text is well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Social inequalities are unfair differences in wealth, status and opportunity among groups.
sla_notes_details: Learners examine how a selected text portrays racial discrimination, wage inequality, homelessness, inequality in education, gender and class divisions. They analyse how settings, contrast between characters, dialogue and symbolism reveal injustice, and discuss possible reforms.
sla_notes_illustrations: A novel that contrasts a wealthy family's mansion with a nearby slum depicts economic inequality.
sla_notes_daily_life: The topic helps learners to recognise and challenge inequality in their communities.
sla_exercise: Give two forms of social inequality.::Racial discrimination and wage inequality.||How can contrast reveal inequality?::By placing rich and poor lives side by side.||What is homelessness?::Lack of a permanent place to live.||Suggest a reform for inequality in education.::Equal access to quality schooling.

specific_competence_name: Analyse the nexus between literature and politics, aesthetics and social inequalities
learning_activity_name: Explore the use of stylistic features to create aesthetics in a selected literary text
sla_name: Stylistic features creating aesthetics
sla_assessment_criteria: The use of stylistic features to create aesthetics in a selected literary text is well explored.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Aesthetics refers to the beauty and artistic quality of a literary work.
sla_notes_details: Stylistic features that create aesthetics include diction, imagery, figures of speech (metaphor, simile, personification), sound devices (alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia and rhyme), rhythm, symbolism, sentence variety, tone and structure. Learners identify the features in a text, and explain how they create beauty, mood and emphasis.
sla_notes_illustrations: Alliteration in: The silent, shining stream slid softly past, creates a soothing musical effect.
sla_notes_daily_life: Appreciating aesthetics increases enjoyment of poetry, songs and speeches.
sla_exercise: Define aesthetics.::The beauty or artistic quality of a work.||What is alliteration?::Repetition of initial consonant sounds.||What is onomatopoeia?::Words that imitate sounds, e.g. buzz.||What effect does rhythm create?::A musical flow and emphasis.

specific_competence_name: Evaluate the effectiveness of various elements of form in shaping meaning
learning_activity_name: Discuss the author’s choice and use of setting in a selected literary work
sla_name: Author's choice and use of setting
sla_assessment_criteria: The author’s choice and use of setting in a selected literary work is well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio- visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An author's choice of setting is deliberate and supports the meaning of the work.
sla_notes_details: Learners discuss the time, place and social environment of the text and examine why the author chose them, how they reflect themes, shape characters' choices, symbolise ideas and create atmosphere. They also consider changes of setting during the story and their effect.
sla_notes_illustrations: A story set in a refugee camp emphasises themes of survival, loss and hope.
sla_notes_daily_life: Setting analysis helps readers to appreciate the context of films and stories.
sla_exercise: Why does an author choose a certain setting?::To support theme, mood and character development.||What is atmosphere?::The mood created by the setting.||Give one symbolic setting.::A dark forest to symbolise danger.||What is a change of setting used for?::To show development or contrast.

specific_competence_name: Evaluate the effectiveness of various elements of form in shaping meaning
learning_activity_name: Examine the author’s development of plot and characterisation in a selected literary work
sla_name: Author's development of plot and characterisation
sla_assessment_criteria: The author’s development of plot and characterisation in a selected literary work is well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Plot and characterisation are the core structures by which authors create narrative and people in a work.
sla_notes_details: Learners analyse the sequence and causation of events, structure (linear, non-linear), subplots, suspense and resolution, and how characters are introduced, revealed and changed through description, dialogue, action and others' comments. They evaluate how well plot and character work together and how believable they are.
sla_notes_illustrations: A character who starts as a timid clerk and becomes a courageous whistle-blower shows development through key events.
sla_notes_daily_life: The analysis is useful for evaluating films, dramas and biographies.
sla_exercise: What is a subplot?::A secondary story within the main plot.||Give two ways of revealing character.::Dialogue and actions.||What is a round character?::A complex character who develops.||What does non-linear plot mean?::Events are not told in chronological order.

specific_competence_name: Evaluate the effectiveness of various elements of form in shaping meaning
learning_activity_name: Discuss the author’s choice and use of rhetorical devices in a selected literary work
sla_name: Author's choice and use of rhetorical devices
sla_assessment_criteria: The author’s choice of rhetorical devices in a selected literary work is well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Rhetorical devices are techniques used to persuade, emphasise and move readers.
sla_notes_details: They include rhetorical questions, repetition, parallelism, antithesis, irony, hyperbole, apostrophe, understatement, analogy and appeals to emotion, logic and ethics. Learners identify their use in a text, discuss the author's purpose in using them and assess the effect on tone and argument.
sla_notes_illustrations: The rhetorical question: How long shall we suffer in silence? involves the audience and encourages action.
sla_notes_daily_life: Rhetoric appears in political speeches, advertisements and sermons.
sla_exercise: What is antithesis?::Placing opposite ideas together for contrast.||Give an example of a rhetorical question.::How long shall we wait?||What is hyperbole?::Deliberate exaggeration.||Why do authors use rhetoric?::To persuade and emphasise.

specific_competence_name: Use literary works to build rational arguments and judgments
learning_activity_name: Assess moral dilemmas depicted in a literary text
sla_name: Moral dilemmas depicted in a literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Moral dilemmas depicted in a literary text are assessed effectively.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio- visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A moral dilemma is a situation in which a character must choose between two conflicting moral choices.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify the dilemma, the values in conflict (loyalty against honesty, duty against love, self-interest against justice), the alternatives, the character's decision and its consequences. They assess whether the decision was justified and discuss what readers learn about human nature and ethics.
sla_notes_illustrations: A judge must decide whether to punish his own son for a crime, torn between justice and family loyalty.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reflecting on dilemmas helps learners to make ethical decisions in life.
sla_exercise: Define moral dilemma.::A difficult choice between two conflicting moral values.||Give two values that may conflict.::Loyalty and honesty.||How can a decision be assessed?::By its reasons and consequences.||Why include dilemmas in literature?::To provoke thought about ethics.

specific_competence_name: Use literary works to build rational arguments and judgments
learning_activity_name: Discuss the conflicts portrayed in a literary text and how they are resolved
sla_name: Conflicts and their resolution in a literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Conflicts and their resolutions presented in a literary text are analysed correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Conflict is the struggle between opposing forces, and resolution is how it is settled.
sla_notes_details: Types of conflict are internal (person against self), interpersonal (person against person), social (person against society) and external (person against nature or fate). Learners identify causes, escalation, climax and resolution, and discuss whether resolution is reached through dialogue, force, sacrifice or compromise, and what message the resolution gives.
sla_notes_illustrations: Two neighbours quarrel over a boundary, and the conflict is resolved through mediation by elders.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding conflict resolution supports peaceful living.
sla_exercise: Name two types of conflict.::Internal and social.||Give one way conflicts are resolved.::Dialogue or mediation.||What is the climax of a conflict?::Its most intense point.||What does resolution show?::The outcome and message of the story.

specific_competence_name: Use literary works to build rational arguments and judgments
learning_activity_name: Assess various interpretations of a literary text
sla_name: Various interpretations of a literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Various interpretations of a literary text are effectively assessed.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A literary text can be interpreted in different ways depending on the reader's perspective.
sla_notes_details: Learners study how readers' background, gender, culture, historical period and theoretical approach lead to different meanings, and how ambiguity, symbolism and open endings allow multiple readings. They compare interpretations, assess their strength using textual evidence and logic, and justify their own view.
sla_notes_illustrations: The closing image of a locked door may be read as loss of freedom or as protection, and the reader decides using evidence.
sla_notes_daily_life: Accepting several viewpoints promotes tolerance and critical thinking.
sla_exercise: Why can texts have multiple meanings?::Because readers differ and texts may be ambiguous.||How do we judge an interpretation?::By textual evidence and logic.||What is an open ending?::An ending that leaves the outcome unresolved.||Name one factor that influences interpretation.::The reader's culture or background.

specific_competence_name: Use literature to adapt and manage new communicative contexts
learning_activity_name: Explain different communicative contexts exhibited in a selected literary text
sla_name: Communicative contexts in a literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Different communicative contexts exhibited in a selected literary text are clearly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|Audio/ audio- visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A communicative context is the situation in which communication occurs, including participants, setting, purpose and relationship.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify contexts such as formal meetings, family conversation, courtroom, market, letters and public speeches in a selected text, and study how language, register, tone, politeness and body language change with the context and the relationships between characters.
sla_notes_illustrations: A character who speaks respectfully to an elder and casually to a friend shows awareness of context.
sla_notes_daily_life: Awareness of context helps learners communicate suitably at home, school and work.
sla_exercise: Define communicative context.::The situation in which communication takes place.||Give two factors that determine register.::Audience and purpose.||How may a character speak to an elder?::Respectfully and formally.||What shows a change of context in a text?::A change in setting, participants or tone.

specific_competence_name: Use literature to adapt and manage new communicative contexts
learning_activity_name: Use a selected literary text to examine the communications of a given character in different contexts
sla_name: Communication of a character in different contexts
sla_assessment_criteria: Character’s communications in different contexts in a selected literary text are well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Characters adapt their communication as contexts change, and this reveals their personality.
sla_notes_details: Learners select a character and examine his or her speech across contexts: at home, in public, under pressure or in conflict, noting diction, tone, silence, non-verbal communication and effect on other characters. They evaluate whether the character communicates effectively and consistently, and what this tells about the character's role and growth.
sla_notes_illustrations: A leader who speaks gently to the villagers but harshly to his workers shows a two-sided character.
sla_notes_daily_life: The analysis builds communication and interpersonal skills.
sla_exercise: What does a character's speech reveal?::Personality, status and attitude.||What is non-verbal communication?::Communication through gestures and expressions.||Give an example of consistent communication.::A person who speaks honestly in every context.||Why analyse a character in different contexts?::To understand the character fully.

specific_competence_name: Identify opportunities created by literary works

sla_name: Opportunities created by literature
sla_assessment_criteria: Various opportunities created by literature are sufficiently surveyed.

sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Literature provides career and income opportunities.
sla_notes_details: Opportunities include writing (novels, poetry, scripts, journalism), editing, publishing, printing, sales and marketing, publicity, teaching, translation, acting, directing, scriptwriting, blogging, book reviewing, and running libraries and bookshops. Learners survey these and the skills each requires, as well as challenges such as copyright and piracy.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who writes and publishes a poetry collection engages in writing, editing, printing and marketing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Literary careers contribute to employment and to the creative economy.
sla_exercise: Name two careers in literature.::Editor and publisher.||What is piracy?::Illegal copying and selling of works.||Which skill does a scriptwriter need?::Creative writing for stage or screen.||How can literature create self-employment?::By writing, publishing or performing one's own works.

specific_competence_name: Identify opportunities created by literary works
learning_activity_name: Identify various opportunities depicted in a selected literary text
sla_name: Opportunities depicted in a selected literary text
sla_assessment_criteria: Various opportunities depicted in a selected literary text are clearly identified.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Literary texts show characters who identify and use opportunities in their environment.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify opportunities such as education, farming, trade, migration, leadership roles and talents, and how characters respond to them through hard work, creativity, risk-taking or wrong choices. They discuss the challenges that block opportunities and what readers can learn.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a novel a girl uses a scholarship opportunity to become a doctor and helps her community.
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising opportunities encourages youth to take initiative.
sla_exercise: Give one opportunity that a character may use.::Education or trade.||What can block an opportunity?::Poverty or discrimination.||What quality helps a character use opportunities?::Hard work and creativity.||What can readers learn?::To seize opportunities responsibly.

sla_name: Designing, writing, revising and editing a script for stage performance
sla_assessment_criteria: Script for stage performance is well designed, written and edited.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A script is the written text of a play, containing dialogue and stage directions.
sla_notes_details: Steps include selecting the idea, planning characters, setting and scenes, writing dialogue that reveals character and advances plot, adding stage directions and props, dividing into acts and scenes, revising for clarity and dramatic effect, editing language and formatting (speaker's name, colon, dialogue, directions in brackets), and rehearsing to test the script.
sla_notes_illustrations: NEEMA: (looking at the empty granary) The rains failed again, Baba. What shall we eat? BABA: (softly) We shall share, my child, as our ancestors did.
sla_notes_daily_life: Scriptwriting skills apply to drama clubs, radio plays and film.
sla_exercise: What are stage directions?::Instructions about actions, tone and setting in a script.||Name two parts of a script.::Dialogue and stage directions.||Why revise a script?::To improve dramatic effect and clarity.||What is a scene?::A division of an act with a single setting or action.

specific_competence_name: Identify opportunities created by literary works
learning_activity_name: Adapt an episode or extract from a selected literary text on the stage
sla_name: Adapting an episode from a literary text for the stage
sla_assessment_criteria: Episode or extract from a selected literary text is well adapted on stage.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Selected novels, plays and poems
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Adaptation is the process of changing a work from one form, such as a novel, into another, such as a play.
sla_notes_details: The adapter selects an episode, identifies key characters and conflicts, turns narration into dialogue and action, sets scenes, considers stage limits of space, props and time, keeps the spirit and message of the original, and rehearses and performs. Learners consider costumes, lighting, music and audience.
sla_notes_illustrations: An extract from a novel in which two brothers quarrel is converted into a scene using dialogue and movement.
sla_notes_daily_life: Adaptation skills support drama festivals and community theatre.
sla_exercise: Define adaptation.::Changing a work from one form to another.||What replaces narration in a play?::Dialogue and action.||Name one stage limitation.::Limited space or props.||Why keep the original message?::To remain faithful to the author's work.

specific_competence_name: Compose original literary works
